title: Variables and Values
description: Master how let and const store and reference values in memory, how variable reassignment operates, why const protects program invariants, and how to write clear, predictable state declarations.

objectives.statement: Differentiate between const (immutable identifier binding) and let (reassignable variable binding).
Predict runtime behavior and TypeError exceptions when attempting to reassign const bindings.
Author and refactor JavaScript variable declarations using appropriate let and const keywords to manage evolving state.

content.title: Naming and Storing Values in Memory
content.hook: Programs do not just perform calculations; they remember facts, track state, and pass data between different operations.
content.context: In JavaScript, a variable is a named binding to a value in memory. Modern JavaScript provides two primary keywords for declaring variables: const for bindings that must never be reassigned, and let for bindings that evolve over time.
goals: Understand how variables give readable names to values stored in memory.
Distinguish immutable identifier bindings (const) from reassignable variables (let).
Prevent common TypeError runtime exceptions caused by illegal const reassignments.
Author clean, intentional variable declarations for application state.

content.title: Mental Model: Variable Bindings as Storage Labels
content.description: Visual diagram comparing let score (a flexible label pointing to box 10, then repointed to box 20) versus const maxLives (a locked label permanently welded to box 3; attempting to repoint causes a runtime TypeError).

content.prompt: What is logged to the console after executing this sequence of statements?

hints.content: Follow the sequence of assignments from top to bottom: score starts at 10, then is replaced with 25, then evaluates 25 + 5.
Because score is declared with let, reassignment is completely valid.

feedback.correct: Correct! Since score is declared with let, its binding can be updated. 25 + 5 evaluates to 30.
feedback.incorrect: Trace line by line: score begins as 10, gets reassigned to 25, then evaluates 25 + 5 = 30.

options.text: A TypeError exception is thrown because const bindings cannot be reassigned.
JavaScript automatically converts maxCapacity into a let variable and updates it to 75.
The reassignment is silently ignored and maxCapacity remains 50.
A SyntaxError is thrown because numbers cannot exceed 50.

hints.content: const stands for constant identifier binding. What exception type is raised when modifying a constant binding?

feedback.correct: Exactly right. Reassigning a const identifier raises an uncaught TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
feedback.incorrect: const creates a strict immutable binding. Attempting to assign a new value with = triggers a runtime TypeError.

content.question: What is the recommended professional standard for choosing between const and let when declaring variables in modern JavaScript?

options.text: Default to const for all declarations; only use let when you know the variable must be reassigned.
Default to let for everything because it provides maximum flexibility.
Use var for global variables and const only for numbers.
Omit keywords entirely so JavaScript creates global variables automatically.

hints.content: Const-by-default communicates intent to other developers and prevents accidental rebinding bugs.

feedback.correct: Spot on! 'const by default, let when needed' makes code predictable, prevents accidental re-binding, and documents that a name stays tied to its value.
feedback.incorrect: Modern best practices emphasize 'const by default' to prevent unintended reassignment bugs and clarify developer intent.

content.title: Declare and Update Course Progress State
content.prompt:
Create and update state variables for a learner dashboard:
1. Declare a constant `courseName` set to `'JavaScript Fundamentals'`.
2. Declare a constant `maxPoints` set to `100`.
3. Declare a reassignable variable `currentPoints` initialized to `0`.
4. Declare a reassignable variable `isPassed` initialized to `false`.
5. Create a function `addScore(points)` that adds `points` to `currentPoints` and updates `isPassed` to `true` if `currentPoints >= 70`.

testCases.description: currentPoints is initialized and updated through addScore
isPassed updates to true when currentPoints >= 70

hints.content: Use const courseName = 'JavaScript Fundamentals'; and const maxPoints = 100; for values that never change.
Use let currentPoints = 0; and let isPassed = false; so they can be reassigned inside addScore.
Inside addScore(points), write: currentPoints = currentPoints + points; isPassed = currentPoints >= 70;

feedback.correct: Excellent work! You cleanly separated immutable configuration constants from mutable application state variables.
feedback.incorrect: Review your declarations: ensure courseName and maxPoints use const, while currentPoints and isPassed use let so addScore can reassign them.

content.prompt: Why is 'const by default, let when needed' such a powerful discipline in professional software engineering? How does declaring a variable with const reduce the cognitive burden on a developer reading your code?

feedback.correct: Well articulated! When readers see const, they have the guarantee that the identifier will never be rebound to a different value downstream, drastically simplifying mental execution tracing.
feedback.incorrect: Please articulate your reflection with at least 50 characters, focusing on how const guarantees binding immutability and clarifies developer intent.

content.title: Variables and Values Mastery
takeaways: const creates an immutable identifier binding that prevents reassignment and protects application constants.
let creates a reassignable variable binding intended for evolving state and accumulators.
Reassigning a const variable throws an uncaught TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
Adopting 'const by default' documents intent and eliminates whole classes of accidental reassignment defects.
